content.title: About
content.content: Beef liver is the organ meat of cattle, packed with nutrients. It has a tender, slightly bitter flavor and a soft texture when cooked. Liver is used in many cuisines: pan‑fried, stewed, in pâtés, and soups.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef liver contains more than 20 vitamins and minerals, including vitamins A, B12, iron, and copper.
In many cultures liver is considered a delicacy and is often served on special occasions.
The liver can accumulate toxins, so it should be cooked thoroughly.
Vitamin A content in liver exceeds the daily requirement by 10‑30 times.
Some traditional recipes use liver for homemade sausages and meatloaf.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: High in iron
items.content: The iron in liver is highly bioavailable and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Including B12, B6, and folate, they are essential for red blood cell formation and energy metabolism.

items.title: Trace minerals
items.content: Copper, zinc, and selenium contribute to the body’s antioxidant systems.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: Liver fits well into low‑carb diets while providing a substantial amount of protein.

items.title: High vitamin A content
items.content: Excessive consumption can lead to hypervitaminosis A, especially in pregnant women.

items.title: Cholesterol levels
items.content: Liver is cholesterol‑rich; individuals with high cholesterol should limit intake.

items.title: Potential toxins
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking may allow harmful substances to remain.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some people may be allergic to beef liver.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Liver can be pan‑fried, stewed, baked, or made into pâté. Before cooking, rinse, remove any membranes, and cut into bite‑size pieces. Soaking in milk or water can mellow the flavor. Serve with onions, vegetables, or as a spread on toast.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh beef liver in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for no more than 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C up to 3 months. Before use, check the smell: fresh liver has a mild meaty aroma, without sour or putrid notes.

content.title: About
content.content: Breadnut (Brosimum alicastrum), also called “palm nut” or “Mexican bread,” is the edible seed of a tropical tree native to Mexico, Guatemala and Belize. The seeds have a mild, slightly sweet flavor reminiscent of fresh bread and are used as a grain, flour or dried fruit in cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Breadnut was a staple food for ancient Maya and Aztec civilizations.
The seeds can be stored for several years without losing nutritional value when kept dry.
Breadnut trees can reach up to 30 m in height and have broad, dense crowns.
Seeds are often used in gluten‑free recipes as a wheat substitute.
Traditional Mexican medicine uses the seeds to aid digestion.

items.title: Rich in complex carbohydrates
items.content: The seeds provide slowly digestible carbs that give sustained energy and fullness.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports normal bowel function and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are essential for blood formation and muscle function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Makes it suitable for people monitoring blood sugar levels.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Phenolic substances help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to breadnut seeds.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking the seeds before use is recommended.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Seeds are relatively calorie‑dense, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Mycotoxin contamination
items.content: Improper storage can lead to mold growth; keep seeds in a dry, cool environment.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Breadnut seeds can be boiled, roasted, ground into flour, or eaten as dried fruit. They are added to porridges, baked goods, soups, and salads. Soaking the seeds in water for 8–12 hours softens them and reduces phytic acid.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry seeds in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent mold development.

content.title: About
content.content: Collard greens are a leafy vegetable from the Brassicaceae family, originally cultivated in the Mediterranean region. Fresh leaves are typically cooked by steaming, boiling, or simmering without added fat, preserving their bright green color and crisp texture. Collards are rich in vitamins, minerals, and dietary fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Collards belong to the same family as cabbage, broccoli, and Brussels sprouts.
Leaves can grow up to 60 cm long, and stalks may reach 1.5 m.
In traditional Southern U.S. cuisine collards are often served with smoked meat, but they can be prepared fat‑free by simply boiling in salted water.
High chlorophyll content makes them an excellent source of antioxidants.
Collards are frequently used in children’s meals because their mild flavor is well accepted.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: One cup of cooked collard greens provides over 800 % of the daily value for vitamin K, essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: High in vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene in the leaves converts to vitamin A, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C adds antioxidant protection and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Mineral dense
items.content: Collards contain calcium, iron, magnesium, and potassium, which are important for muscle, nerve, and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion, satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Collard greens contain oxalates that may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Interaction with anticoagulants
items.content: Large amounts of vitamin K can reduce the effectiveness of blood‑thinning medications.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: As with many leafy greens, collards may carry pesticide residues; thorough washing before cooking is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Collard greens can be boiled in salted water for 5‑7 minutes, steamed, or quickly sautéed without oil using a splash of broth. They are added to soups, stews, salads, and smoothies. For a milder taste, soak the leaves in cold water before cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh leaves in a bag or container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Cooked portions can be frozen in airtight bags for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg roll, meatless is a vegetarian roll snack made from rice paper, vegetables, tofu and aromatic spices. It has a crispy outer layer and a tender filling that mimics a traditional egg roll without meat or eggs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The vegetarian version is popular in Asian cuisine as a meat‑free alternative.
To achieve a crunchy crust, rolls are often deep‑fried at 180 °C for 2–3 minutes.
Tofu in the filling provides plant‑based protein and makes the dish more filling.
A blend of soy sauce, ginger and garlic gives the roll its characteristic savory flavor.
Egg roll, meatless is commonly served with sweet chili sauce or soy sauce.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Tofu and vegetables supply a good amount of protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Absence of meat and eggs makes the roll less fatty than traditional versions.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Carrots, cabbage and peppers contain vitamins B6 and B9, important for metabolism.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Cabbage and carrots aid digestion and promote satiety.

items.title: Low cholesterol
items.content: No animal products means the dish is suitable for cholesterol‑lowering diets.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Tofu may trigger allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to soy.

items.title: High sodium in sauces
items.content: Soy sauce and ready‑made seasonings can increase salt intake; choose low‑sodium options.

items.title: Trans fats from frying
items.content: Frequent deep‑frying can generate trans fats; limit the number of fried rolls.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Improper storage or reheating may lead to bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Egg roll, meatless can be enjoyed hot as a snack, served with soy sauce, sweet chili or ginger dipping sauce. Slice into bite‑size pieces for appetizers or as a side to a main dish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked rolls in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in the oven or skillet to restore crispness. Freezing is not recommended as the wrapper loses its texture.

content.title: About
content.content: The egg sandwich on wheat bread consists of two slices of whole‑grain wheat bread, a soft boiled egg, a leaf of lettuce, and a light sauce. It is a nutritious and quick snack suitable for breakfast or a light lunch.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wheat bread provides slow‑release energy thanks to complex carbohydrates.
Eggs are one of the most affordable sources of high‑quality protein.
Sandwiches became popular in the United States in the early 20th century with the rise of factory bakeries.
Adding lettuce boosts vitamin K and fiber content.
Traditional sauce often combines mayonnaise, mustard, and a splash of lemon juice.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs contain all essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and whole‑grain bread provide vitamins B2, B6, and B12, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Egg yolk is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids, which support heart health.

items.title: Fiber and minerals
items.content: Wheat bread supplies dietary fiber, iron, and magnesium, aiding normal digestion.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Unlike sweet pastries, this sandwich contains virtually no added sugar.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg whites.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolk contains cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume in moderation.

items.title: Gluten in bread
items.content: Wheat bread contains gluten, which can be problematic for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Sauce and bread can add salt; those monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt options.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is easy to eat by hand, preferably cut in half. It can be served warm (with toasted bread) or cold. Add fresh vegetables such as tomato or cucumber for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Keep bread in a dry place, and boiled eggs refrigerated if prepared ahead of time.

ice-cream-sundae-fruit-topping.title: Ice Cream Sundae with Fruit Topping

content.title: About
content.content: Ice cream sundae with fruit topping is a classic dessert consisting of vanilla ice cream scoops drenched in rich chocolate sauce and generously topped with fresh fruits, berries, and sometimes nuts. The fruit topping adds sweetness, a hint of acidity, and a vibrant color palette.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first sundae appeared in the United States in the early 20th century as a street‑side treat.
Traditional fruit toppings often include strawberry, banana, kiwi and blueberry.
In some countries the sundae is served with caramel sauce instead of chocolate.
Vegan versions use coconut‑milk ice cream and unsweetened fruit purees.

items.title: Vitamins and Antioxidants
items.content: Fresh fruits are rich in vitamin C, vitamin A and polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: The dairy base of the ice cream supplies calcium, essential for bones and teeth.

items.title: Energy Boost
items.content: Carbohydrates from the fruit and fats from the ice cream quickly replenish energy after physical activity.

items.title: Dietary Fiber
items.content: Fruits add dietary fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Sugar Content
items.content: Both ice cream and fruit topping can be high in sugar, which is a concern for diabetics or those watching their weight.

items.title: Lactose Intolerance
items.content: Traditional ice cream contains lactose; lactose‑intolerant individuals should choose dairy‑free alternatives.

items.title: Nut Allergy
items.content: If nuts are included in the topping, they may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive people.

items.title: Fruit Acidity
items.content: Acidic fruits can irritate sensitive teeth or the stomach.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sundae in tall glasses, layering ice cream, sauce and fruit. Top with whipped cream, chopped nuts or sprinkles. For a lighter version, use frozen berries instead of fresh fruit.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep ice cream in the freezer at –18 °C in an airtight container. Store the fruit topping separately in the refrigerator and use within 2‑3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: A blend of shellfish (shrimp, mussels, squid) with vegetables such as carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy greens, without potatoes or soy‑based sauce. The product cooks quickly, retains maximum nutrients and fits a variety of dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shellfish are rich in high‑quality protein and omega‑3 fatty acids.
Broccoli contains sulforaphane, a compound that supports cellular detoxification.
Dark‑green leafy greens (spinach, kale) are among the best sources of vitamin K.
Carrots are an excellent source of beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
The soy‑free formulation is suitable for people with soy allergy.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Omega‑3s from shellfish help lower triglycerides and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Immune system boost
items.content: Vitamin C from broccoli and beta‑carotene from carrots enhance immune defenses.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Vitamin K and calcium from leafy greens contribute to bone mineralization.

items.title: Eye health
items.content: Beta‑carotene and lutein from carrots and leafy greens protect eyes from oxidative stress.

items.title: Reduced risk of chronic disease
items.content: Antioxidants and polyphenols in the mix help combat free radicals.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp, mussels or squid.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: If the product is pre‑salted, monitor total sodium intake, especially for hypertension.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large portions of shellfish can cause upset in people with sensitive stomachs.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Certain shellfish may contain trace amounts of mercury; choose reputable suppliers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Quickly stir‑fry the mix in olive oil, add to pasta, rice, couscous, or use as a filling for wraps. Keep vegetables crisp by not overcooking. Finish with fresh herbs and a squeeze of lemon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Freeze in portion‑sized bags for up to 2 months. Discard if you notice an ammonia smell or color change.

content.title: About
content.content: Yogurt, nonfat milk and fruit is a combination of a low‑fat dairy product, live probiotic cultures, and fresh fruit, often enjoyed as a healthy breakfast or snack. Nonfat milk provides protein and calcium without extra fat, yogurt adds probiotics, and fruit contributes vitamins, minerals and natural sweetness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The yogurt‑fruit combo is popular worldwide, from Greek yogurt with honey to Scandinavian fruit bowls.
Nonfat milk retains almost all the nutrients of whole milk while containing virtually no fat.
Probiotics in yogurt can support a healthy gut microbiome and improve digestion.
Seasonal fresh fruits are often used, enhancing flavor and vitamin content.
Yogurt with fruit is frequently fortified with vitamin D and calcium for bone health.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Nonfat milk and yogurt together provide a high‑quality protein source essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Probiotic content
items.content: Live cultures in yogurt promote gut health, aiding digestion and immune function.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Fruit adds vitamin C, potassium and antioxidants, while milk supplies calcium and vitamin D.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Using nonfat milk makes the product suitable for low‑fat diets without sacrificing nutrition.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The blend of protein, probiotics and fruit fiber helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort, although some yogurts contain reduced lactose.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein or whey requires complete avoidance of the product.

items.title: Added sugar
items.content: Pre‑made mixes can contain added sugars; choose unsweetened or low‑sugar versions.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Yogurt’s acidity may cause mild stomach upset in individuals with sensitive digestion.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the yogurt, nonfat milk and fruit as a standalone snack, stir it into granola, blend into smoothies, or use as a topping for pancakes. Mix yogurt with sliced berries, banana or kiwi, and optionally drizzle a little honey for extra sweetness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the product in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3‑5 days. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours to prevent bacterial growth.
